I've been doing this for 26 years. I know this land. My father farmed it before me, and I learned by watching and doing. I don't read the agriculture books — I watch the crops, I talk to neighbors at the well, I remember what happened last year and the year before.

My 7 mu splits naturally: 5 mu stays in the wheat-maize rotation the way it always has, and 2 mu I keep for cotton. That's how my father did it and it spreads my risk — if grain prices drop, cotton helps; if the cotton gets sick, the grain keeps us fed.

For the **wheat** going in this October, I'll plough deep like I always do before planting — breaks up the hardpan. I'll use the improved variety the village supply station sells, same as last few years, yields well enough. I'll put down base fertilizer at planting and topdress at jointing. Four irrigations: winter water to help establishment, green-up water, jointing water, and grain-fill water. That's what the land needs here with these dry springs.

For **summer maize** right after wheat harvest in June — I have to move fast, no time to waste. I use hybrid seed, everyone around here does, the yields are much better than the old types. I rotary till to break the wheat stubble and get seed in the ground quickly. Two irrigations if the summer rains are weak, which they often are.

For the **cotton** — this is the demanding crop. Cotton needs watching. Five pesticide sprays at minimum — aphids come early, then bollworm later. I plough that plot in spring and irrigate three times through the season. My wife and sometimes my son help with the topping and picking since they're around more than the hired days.

With some family off-farm, I keep inputs moderate — I can't overspend on fertilizer I don't need to pay back wages. But I don't cut corners on seed or pest control. Those two decisions cost you the whole season if you get them wrong.
